2-in-1 adaptive design

Source: vignettes/two-in-one.Rmd
two-in-one.Rmd
library(CorOncoEndpoints)

In the 2-in-1 design of Chen et al. (2018), a statistic X at an interim analysis decides whether a phase 2 trial is kept as it is or expanded into a phase 3 trial. With standardized statistics Y at the end of the small trial and Z at the end of the large trial, the study is positive if X < c and Y > w, or if X >= c and Z > w, where c is the expansion cutpoint and w the critical value of a one-sided test. Chen et al. showed that the type I error is controlled for every c when the statistics are bivariate normal and X is at least as strongly correlated with Y as with Z. When X is based on response, Y on PFS and Z on OS, these correlations follow from the joint distribution of the endpoints and the timing of the analyses, and the generator allows them to be evaluated. This vignette uses a smaller number of simulated trials than the article on the package.

Design and groups

The small trial has 120 patients enrolled over 12 months. X is the standardized difference in response rates among the first 90 patients, 3 months after the last of them has entered, and counts only responses observed by then. The small trial ends at 70 PFS events, and Y is the log-rank statistic for PFS. In an expansion, 380 further patients are enrolled at 30 per month from month 12 or from the interim analysis, whichever is later, so that no patient of the expansion enters before the decision. The large trial ends at 330 deaths, with Z the log-rank statistic for OS. Under the global null hypothesis, both groups have the same distribution:

ctl <- OncoArm(pfs.median = 6, orr = 0.30, resp.cor = 0.40, death.prop = 0.15,
               os.median = 15, pps.hr.resp = 0.6, resp.timing = "ttr",
               resp.tau = 1.5, ttr.median = 2.5)
arms <- list(Control = ctl, Treatment = ctl)

Simulated trials

Both parts of every trial are generated, and whether the expansion takes place is decided afterwards from X, so that every cutpoint is evaluated on the same trials. The interim analysis takes place 3 months after the entry of the 90th patient of the small part, which can be after month 12. The expansion enrolls 30 patients per month until its 380 patients are enrolled, starting at month 12 or at the interim analysis, whichever is later: it is generated from time 0 (a.time = 0) and shifted to its start in each trial. It uses another random-number stream than the small part.

nsim <- 1000
small <- rOncoEndpoints(nsim = nsim, n = c(60, 60), arms = arms,
                        a.time = c(0, 12), seed = 2018)
# time of the interim analysis: 3 months after the entry of the 90th patient
small <- small[order(small$sim, small$accrual_time), ]
first90 <- small[ave(small$accrual_time, small$sim, FUN = seq_along) <= 90, ]
t_x <- tapply(first90$accrual_time, first90$sim, max) + 3
# expansion: 30 patients per month from month 12 or from the interim analysis,
# whichever is later
start <- pmax(12, as.vector(t_x))
expansion <- rOncoEndpoints(nsim = nsim, n = c(190, 190), arms = arms,
                            a.time = 0, a.rate = 30, seed = 2018, stream = 1)
expansion$accrual_time <- expansion$accrual_time + start[expansion$sim]
expansion$pfs_calendar_time <- expansion$accrual_time + expansion$pfs_tte
expansion$os_calendar_time <- expansion$accrual_time + expansion$os_tte
large <- rbind(small, expansion)
summary(start)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   12.00   12.00   12.00   12.15   12.25   13.37

The interim analysis took place after month 12 in 45% of the trials; in these trials the expansion started at the interim analysis.

The statistics are computed with CutoffData() and EventTime(), the pooled test of two proportions for X, and survival::survdiff() for the log-rank statistics, all oriented so that positive values favor the treatment group.

# pooled Z statistic for the difference in observed response proportions
orr_z <- function(d) {
  x <- tapply(d$response_obs, list(d$sim, d$group), sum)
  m <- tapply(d$response_obs, list(d$sim, d$group), length)
  p <- (x[, "Control"] + x[, "Treatment"]) / (m[, "Control"] + m[, "Treatment"])
  se <- sqrt(p * (1 - p) * (1 / m[, "Control"] + 1 / m[, "Treatment"]))
  ifelse(se > 0, (x[, "Treatment"] / m[, "Treatment"] -
                    x[, "Control"] / m[, "Control"]) / se, 0)
}
# log-rank statistic per simulated trial
logrank_z <- function(d, tte, event) {
  vapply(split(d, d$sim), function(x) {
    s <- survival::survdiff(survival::Surv(time, status) ~ group,
                            data = data.frame(time = x[[tte]], status = x[[event]],
                                              group = x$group))
    -(s$obs[2] - s$exp[2]) / sqrt(s$var[2, 2])
  }, numeric(1))
}
# interim analysis: first 90 patients of the small part, at t_x
X <- orr_z(CutoffData(first90, t_x))
# end of the small trial (70 PFS events) and of the large trial (330 deaths)
Y <- logrank_z(CutoffData(small, EventTime(small, 70, "pfs")), "pfs_tte", "pfs_event")
Z <- logrank_z(CutoffData(large, EventTime(large, 330, "os")), "os_tte", "os_event")
round(cor(cbind(X, Y, Z)), 3)
#>       X     Y     Z
#> X 1.000 0.368 0.149
#> Y 0.368 1.000 0.249
#> Z 0.149 0.249 1.000

The correlation of X with Y is 0.37 and that with Z is 0.15. The interim population overlaps more with the small trial (90 of 120 patients) than with the large trial (90 of 500), and response is more strongly associated with PFS than with OS.

Type I error 

w <- qnorm(0.975)
type1 <- function(cc) mean(ifelse(X >= cc, Z > w, Y > w))
cutpoints <- c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.645, 2, 3)
data.frame(cutpoint = cutpoints,
           expanded = sapply(cutpoints, function(cc) mean(X >= cc)),
           type1 = sapply(cutpoints, type1))
#>   cutpoint expanded type1
#> 1    0.000    0.514 0.018
#> 2    0.500    0.286 0.016
#> 3    1.000    0.151 0.022
#> 4    1.645    0.055 0.027
#> 5    2.000    0.027 0.032
#> 6    3.000    0.003 0.034

With 1000 simulated trials, the Monte Carlo standard error of a type I error rate near 0.025 is about 0.005. For a large cutpoint almost no trial is expanded, and the rate approaches the proportion of trials with Y > w, here 0.034, which differs from 0.025 by 1.8 standard errors; for a small cutpoint it approaches the proportion with Z > w, here 0.028. At the cutpoint 1.645, 6% of the trials were expanded, and the estimated type I error rate was 0.027. A stronger association of response with OS, for example through a longer survival of responders after progression (pps.hr.resp further below 1), increases the correlation of X with Z, and the generator shows how the operating characteristics of a planned design depend on it.

Reference

Chen, C., Anderson, K., Mehrotra, D. V., Rubin, E. H. and Tse, A. (2018). A 2-in-1 adaptive phase 2/3 design for expedited oncology drug development. Contemporary Clinical Trials, 64, 238-242. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cct.2017.09.006
